# Drag on circular cylinders in a tow tank

**Manuscript status:** first draft; author and affiliation details, literature context, uncertainty analysis, and several apparatus details remain to be supplied.

## Abstract

We measured the drag on smooth circular cylinders towed through a water tank at speeds from 0.2 to 1.1 m s⁻¹. Three nominal cylinder diameters (25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm) were tested, with approximately 0.60 m of each cylinder submerged. A calibrated load cell recorded force during each tow. The existing analysis subtracts the mean pre-tow signal and averages the force over a nominal steady interval from 3 to 8 s. Using the projected area based on cylinder diameter and submerged length, water density 998 kg m⁻³, and kinematic viscosity 1.004 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹, the calculated mean drag coefficients were 1.144, 1.153, and 1.178 for the 25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm cylinders, respectively. The corresponding nominal Reynolds-number range is approximately 5.1 × 10³ to 5.6 × 10⁴. These measurements provide a consistent preliminary comparison across cylinder sizes, but interpretation is limited by the use of a single viscosity for water temperatures spanning 13.7–17.6 °C, one tow per speed and size, and unresolved questions about blockage, support forces, and one flagged force record. The results should therefore be regarded as preliminary until these effects and the measurement uncertainty are assessed.

**Keywords:** cylinder drag; tow tank; Reynolds number; force measurement

## 1. Introduction

Circular-cylinder drag is a basic fluid-mechanics problem and a useful test of force-measurement methods. The drag coefficient depends on Reynolds number and on experimental details such as end effects, free-surface proximity, blockage, surface condition, and support interference. A controlled tow-tank measurement can compare the force on cylinders of different diameters over a practical range of speeds.

Here we report an initial analysis of tow-tank measurements on three smooth circular cylinders. The available records comprise ten nominal speeds from 0.2 to 1.1 m s⁻¹ for each cylinder. This draft documents the data reduction presently implemented in the project and reports its direct results. It is not yet a complete comparison with published cylinder-drag data: references, a fuller description of the rig, and corrections and uncertainty estimates remain to be added.

## 2. Experimental methods

### 2.1 Tow tank and test articles

The project notes describe tests in a tow tank approximately 0.9 m wide and 0.75 m deep. Smooth circular cylinders of diameters 25.4 mm (1 in), 38.1 mm (1.5 in), and 50.8 mm (2 in) were tested with a nominal submerged length of 0.60 m. The run log records the target speed and water temperature for each run. Tests on the 25.4 mm cylinder were made on 14 October 2025, those on the 50.8 mm cylinder on 3 November 2025, and those on the 38.1 mm cylinder on 12 March 2026. The recorded water temperatures were 16.9–17.6 °C, 15.0–15.6 °C, and 13.7–14.3 °C, respectively.

The existing records do not specify cylinder material, surface roughness, support geometry, distance from the tank boundaries, tow acceleration profile, or how the 0.60 m wetted length was established. These details should be confirmed and added before submission.

### 2.2 Force measurement and calibration

Drag force was measured with a load cell. The September 2025 calibration file contains applied masses and output voltages and was used for the October and November runs. The March 2026 session followed remounting and recalibration; the processing script uses a sensitivity of 0.0213 V N⁻¹ for this session. The recorded sensitivities are approximately 0.020 V N⁻¹ for the September calibration and 0.0213 V N⁻¹ for March. The calibration fit method, fit uncertainty, loading/unloading behavior, and zero drift are not yet included in the analysis.

For each record, the present processing subtracts the mean voltage before 1 s from the full voltage trace and divides the result by the calibration sensitivity. Mean drag and sample standard deviation are then calculated over 3 < t < 8 s. The older data use comma-separated files; the March files use semicolon-separated fields. The processed files retain one mean and standard deviation per run.

### 2.3 Dimensionless quantities

The Reynolds number and drag coefficient are calculated as

\[
  Re = \frac{U D}{\nu}, \qquad
  C_D = \frac{F_D}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 D L},
\]

where \(U\) is the logged tow speed, \(D\) is cylinder diameter, \(L=0.60\) m is the nominal submerged length, and \(F_D\) is the processed mean force. The denominator uses the projected frontal area \(DL\). The notebook currently takes \(\rho=998\) kg m⁻³ and \(\nu=1.004\times10^{-6}\) m² s⁻¹, corresponding to its comment “20C.” The temperature-dependent viscosity has not yet been applied, so the Reynolds numbers below are nominal values and should be recalculated at the recorded water temperature.

## 3. Results

Thirty runs are present in the run log and processed force files: ten per cylinder, at nominal speeds from 0.2 to 1.1 m s⁻¹. Under the current data reduction, the mean drag coefficient across the ten speeds is 1.144 for the 25.4 mm cylinder, 1.153 for the 38.1 mm cylinder, and 1.178 for the 50.8 mm cylinder. The corresponding ranges across individual runs are 1.094–1.182, 1.105–1.193, and 1.108–1.357. These ranges describe variation across speed points; they are not replicate-based confidence intervals.

![Drag coefficient versus nominal Reynolds number for the three cylinder diameters.](../figures/cd_vs_re.png)

**Figure 1.** Drag coefficient calculated using the fixed 20 °C kinematic viscosity in the analysis notebook. The plotted values are preliminary and do not include a temperature correction or uncertainty bars.

The 2 in series has the largest spread in the calculated coefficient, with its highest value at the 0.8 m s⁻¹ run. The run log independently flags this run because the zero appeared offset after the run. This point should be inspected against the raw time trace and calibration/zero history before it is retained in a final analysis. The other two series show smaller variation in the values calculated by the current procedure. The data support a first comparison of the three test series, but they do not establish a repeatability estimate because each speed-size condition appears only once.

## 4. Discussion

Across the tested range, the current reduction gives coefficients near 1.1–1.2 for all three cylinder sizes. The group means differ by only about 3% from the smallest to largest cylinder. This apparent similarity is a useful initial result, but the experiments were conducted on different dates and at different water temperatures. They also span different Reynolds-number ranges for each cylinder at the same speed. A quantitative conclusion about diameter or Reynolds-number effects requires temperature-corrected properties, an explicit uncertainty budget, and review of the run flagged for zero drift.

Several experimental corrections may matter. The tank width and depth are recorded as 0.9 m and 0.75 m, giving a combined transverse dimension of 1.65 m relative to cylinder diameters of 0.0254–0.0508 m. A blockage correction may be needed, but selecting one requires a clear account of the cylinder orientation, free surface, floor clearance, support, and applicable correction model. The measured load may also include support or end effects; these should be characterized with blank/support runs or an equivalent correction if available.

The reported force standard deviations represent fluctuations within each selected 5 s averaging window. They do not include calibration uncertainty, uncertainty in tow speed, diameter or wetted length, water properties, tare drift, run-to-run variability, or systematic effects. In particular, a single run at each condition cannot quantify repeatability. Future runs should include repeats and a documented tare/zero check before and after each tow.

## 5. Conclusions

An initial reduction of 30 tow-tank runs on smooth circular cylinders gives mean drag coefficients of 1.144, 1.153, and 1.178 for diameters of 25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm, respectively, using a fixed 20 °C viscosity and a 0.60 m projected wetted length. These are preliminary values. The next analysis should use water properties at the logged temperatures, investigate the flagged 2 in run, quantify calibration and force uncertainty, assess tank and support corrections, and add repeat measurements. A literature comparison and full apparatus description are also needed before this can serve as a submission-ready paper.

## Data and code availability

Raw force records, calibration data, the run log, processing scripts, processed force summaries, and the analysis notebook are included in this Calkit project. The analysis should be rerun after resolving the open data-reduction items above.

## Acknowledgments

To be completed.

## References

References to foundational cylinder-drag measurements, the selected blockage correction, and the calibration/measurement methods are to be added. No references have been inferred from the project files.

## Author checklist for the next draft

- Confirm author names, affiliations, and target journal format.
- Add the rig and support geometry, cylinder material/finish, tow speed measurement method, and actual immersion/wetted-length details.
- Recalculate water density and viscosity from each run's recorded water temperature.
- Inspect run 17 and document the decision to retain, correct, or exclude it.
- Quantify calibration fit and drift, force averaging uncertainty, speed and dimensional uncertainty, and repeatability.
- Decide whether blockage, free-surface, end, and support corrections apply, and justify their use.
- Add independent repeat runs and compare against cited literature.

7:We measured the drag on smooth circular cylinders towed through a water tank at speeds from 0.2 to 1.1 m s⁻¹. Three nominal cylinder diameters (25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm) were tested, with approximately 0.60 m of each cylinder submerged. A calibrated load cell recorded force during each tow. The existing analysis subtracts the mean pre-tow signal and averages the force over a nominal steady interval from 3 to 8 s. Using the projected area based on cylinder diameter and submerged length, water density 998 kg m⁻³, and kinematic viscosity 1.004 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹, the calculated mean drag coefficients were 1.144, 1.153, and 1.178 for the 25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm cylinders, respectively. The corresponding nominal Reynolds-number range is approximately 5.1 × 10³ to 5.6 × 10⁴. These measurements provide a consistent preliminary comparison across cylinder sizes, but interpretation is limited by the use of a single viscosity for water temperatures spanning 13.7–17.6 °C, one tow per speed and size, and unresolved questions about blockage, support forces, and one flagged force record. The results should therefore be regarded as preliminary until these effects and the measurement uncertainty are assessed.
40:where \(U\) is the logged tow speed, \(D\) is cylinder diameter, \(L=0.60\) m is the nominal submerged length, and \(F_D\) is the processed mean force. The denominator uses the projected frontal area \(DL\). The notebook currently takes \(\rho=998\) kg m⁻³ and \(\nu=1.004\times10^{-6}\) m² s⁻¹, corresponding to its comment “20C.” The temperature-dependent viscosity has not yet been applied, so the Reynolds numbers below are nominal values and should be recalculated at the recorded water temperature.
44:Thirty runs are present in the run log and processed force files: ten per cylinder, at nominal speeds from 0.2 to 1.1 m s⁻¹. Under the current data reduction, the mean drag coefficient across the ten speeds is 1.144 for the 25.4 mm cylinder, 1.153 for the 38.1 mm cylinder, and 1.178 for the 50.8 mm cylinder. The corresponding ranges across individual runs are 1.094–1.182, 1.105–1.193, and 1.108–1.357. These ranges describe variation across speed points; they are not replicate-based confidence intervals.
48:**Figure 1.** Drag coefficient calculated using the fixed 20 °C kinematic viscosity in the analysis notebook. The plotted values are preliminary and do not include a temperature correction or uncertainty bars.
50:The 2 in series has the largest spread in the calculated coefficient, with its highest value at the 0.8 m s⁻¹ run. The run log independently flags this run because the zero appeared offset after the run. This point should be inspected against the raw time trace and calibration/zero history before it is retained in a final analysis. The other two series show smaller variation in the values calculated by the current procedure. The data support a first comparison of the three test series, but they do not establish a repeatability estimate because each speed-size condition appears only once.
54:Across the tested range, the current reduction gives coefficients near 1.1–1.2 for all three cylinder sizes. The group means differ by only about 3% from the smallest to largest cylinder. This apparent similarity is a useful initial result, but the experiments were conducted on different dates and at different water temperatures. They also span different Reynolds-number ranges for each cylinder at the same speed. A quantitative conclusion about diameter or Reynolds-number effects requires temperature-corrected properties, an explicit uncertainty budget, and review of the run flagged for zero drift.
62:An initial reduction of 30 tow-tank runs on smooth circular cylinders gives mean drag coefficients of 1.144, 1.153, and 1.178 for diameters of 25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm, respectively, using a fixed 20 °C viscosity and a 0.60 m projected wetted length. These are preliminary values. The next analysis should use water properties at the logged temperatures, investigate the flagged 2 in run, quantify calibration and force uncertainty, assess tank and support corrections, and add repeat measurements. A literature comparison and full apparatus description are also needed before this can serve as a submission-ready paper.

The exclusion is based on the contemporaneous run-log note that the zero was offset after this tow; the record remains available in the processed data but is omitted from Figure 1 and summary statistics. The other two series show smaller variation in the values calculated by the current procedure. The data support a first comparison of the three test series, but they do not establish a repeatability estimate because each speed-size condition appears only once.
paper/draft.md:54:Across the tested range, the current reduction gives coefficients near 1.1–1.2 for all three cylinder sizes. The group means differ by about 1% from the smallest to largest cylinder after excluding run 17. This apparent similarity is a useful initial result, but the experiments were conducted on different dates and at different water temperatures. They also span different Reynolds-number ranges for each cylinder at the same speed. A quantitative conclusion about diameter or Reynolds-number effects requires an explicit uncertainty budget and further repeat measurements.
paper/draft.md:62:An initial reduction of 29 accepted tow-tank runs on smooth circular cylinders gives mean drag coefficients of 1.144, 1.153, and 1.159 for diameters of 25.4, 38.1, and 50.8 mm, respectively, using a 0.60 m projected wetted length. Reynolds number was calculated using water viscosity at each run's measured temperature, spanning 4.69 × 10³ to 4.99 × 10⁴. Run 17 was excluded because the run log flags a post-run zero offset. These are preliminary values. Calibration and force uncertainty, tank and support corrections, repeat measurements, a literature comparison, and a full apparatus description are still needed.

Updated the draft to address all three reviews. It now reports the temperature-corrected Reynolds-number range (4.69×10³–4.99×10⁴), states that run 17 was excluded because of the logged post-run zero offset, and gives the revised 2 in mean drag coefficient of 1.159. The abstract includes the Reynolds-number range.

I also updated the analysis notebook and regenerated the drag-coefficient figure without run 17. Notebook outputs were cleared so the old summary values are no longer displayed.
